name: Marcus Aurelius
essay: As I lie here, a device screams at me to rise, shattering the stillness of the morning. What urgency is this, that I must be jarred from my rest like a beast from its lair? Can it truly be said that the passing of time is so precious, so fleeting, that I must be torn from slumber to attend to its every tick? And yet, I submit to this tyranny, day after day, as if the arbitrary chime of this device held some greater significance than the gentle stirrings of my own heart. In this, I am a slave to the whims of a machine, rather than a master of my own soul. The universe unfolds with indifference, heedless of my petty schedules and appointments, and still I rush to answer the summons of this mindless thing, as if my very existence depended on it. I am ashamed of this weakness, and the absurdity of it all.

name: Marcus Aurelius
essay: As I find myself confined in a room with contrived obstacles, I am reminded that true freedom lies not in the physical realm, but in the mind. The artificial challenges that surround me are but a pale reflection of the real struggles that beset us all. And yet, I must acknowledge the fleeting pleasure that comes from overcoming these trivial hurdles. But let us not be deceived, for in the grand tapestry of existence, such diversions are but a minor thread. The hours we spend in such pursuits are lost forever, and the triumphs we achieve are hollow and short-lived. Still, I shall play along, for even in the most frivolous of activities, there lies a lesson to be learned about the human condition, and the fragility of our existence. In the end, it is not the escape that matters, but the journey, and the opportunity to confront our own mortality, and the impermanence of all things.

name: Joan Didion
essay: It is 3:14 in the morning in a hotel room in Omaha. The phone lit up on the nightstand. Someone in London was typing about a coat. Someone in New York was sending an image of a dog. I sat on the edge of the mattress and watched the names appear. Laura. Sam. Laura again. There were fourteen people in the room, though none of them were in Nebraska. They were talking about dinner from three nights ago. They were talking about whether it had rained in Connecticut. I watched the green dot appear beside Laura’s name. I watched the green dot disappear. I thought about the silence before the green dot. I thought about what it meant to have fourteen people in your bedroom at 3:14 in the morning, none of them speaking, all of them typing. You do not leave the room because leaving is an act of violence. Staying is also an act of violence, but it is a quiet one. The screen dimmed. Then Laura typed again. The phone vibrated twice on the faux-wood veneer. It was not an emergency. Nothing was ever an emergency. That was the point.

name: Joan Didion
essay: It was three in the afternoon in the quiet area, which was not quiet, only dimly lit. A sign on the frosted glass said Executive Lounge, but there were no executives, only tired men in unbuttoned shirts drinking lukewarm San Pellegrino from heavy crystal tumblers. The carpet was navy blue with faint silver grid lines, designed to disguise spills. Someone had spilled tomato juice near the espresso machine at eleven that morning. At three, the stain was still there, dark and sticky under the recessed LED lights. A woman in a camel coat was speaking into a silver earpiece about a contract in Zurich. She spoke in a flat, even tone that suggested Zurich was not a place, but merely a set of numbers that had to be moved from one ledger to another before five o'clock. Outside the glass, a line of yellow tugs moved across the tarmac in the grey rain, moving baggage from nowhere to nowhere. The room smelled of ozone and hot carpet fibers. They tell you that you are waiting for a flight to London, or Tokyo, or Frankfurt. You sit on a low leather sofa that has lost its shape and you drink the cold water and you realize that no one in this room is going anywhere.

name: Nora Ephron
essay: I have spent four hundred dollars on neck cream because of a man named Arthur who listed his height as six foot one and turned out to be five foot eight in thick loafers. We were at the bar at Michael’s on West Fifty-Fifth Street, and he was explaining his divorce while I looked at his forehead and thought about my own lighting. That is what Hinge does. It turns you into a woman who swipes right on a thirty-four-year-old venture capitalist named Chad because he is holding a golden retriever, even though you know perfectly well the dog belongs to his sister. You sit on the sofa in your pajamas at midnight, moving your thumb half an inch to the left, rejecting men because they are wearing wraparound sunglasses or because they used the word adventure as a verb. It feels like catalog shopping, except everything on the page has already been returned once. The trouble is not that it is humiliating, though it is. The trouble is that next Tuesday, when the apartment is quiet, you will open the little yellow icon again, convincing yourself that somewhere in Manhattan there is a man who understands why you hate the sound of people eating apples, and that he is waiting.

name: Nora Ephron
essay: I muted the five of us at nine in the morning on a Tuesday, right after Sarah sent a photo of a turnip. By noon there were forty-two messages, mostly from Jane, who lives on East End Avenue and has never once met a root vegetable she couldn't write three paragraphs about. The trouble with the group is that you cannot leave without committing a public execution. If you press leave, a small grey announcement appears on everyone else’s screen, which is precisely the same as standing up at a dinner party on 74th Street, spitting into the butter dish, and walking out into the rain without your coat. So you stay. You watch three little grey dots jump up and down like a frantic heart monitor while four grown women debate whether eight o'clock is too late for polenta. I spend two hours a day typing ha ha to things that are not funny. I do it because if I stop, they will start another group without me, the one where they talk about my neck. But mostly I do it because I am terrified that if I step out of the noise, even for an afternoon, nobody will notice I went.

name: Franz Kafka
essay: S. had placed the small jar of preserved plums upon the tray precisely where the illuminated arrows indicated, yet the machine, possessing no visible capacity for thought and yet deliberating with an insufferable, polite stillness, immediately flashed a small crimson lamp above its frame to signal that an unscheduled weight had been detected. Although S. knew that he possessed the required coins and that the clerk standing several paces away had seen him place the jar down without any improper intent, it was nonetheless impossible for S. to proceed to the payment slot until this same clerk, who was presently occupied with smoothing the apron of a colleague, chose to touch a master key against the glass, an act that might take only a moment or might require S. to remain standing quietly in the glaring light until closing time. S. did not mind waiting, for he understood that the machine was merely enforcing a rule whose higher logic had simply not been explained to him, and so he adjusted his posture slightly, holding his breath so as not to disturb the scales, entirely convinced that once the red light was extinguished he would be permitted to pay, though he suspected that a second verification would then become necessary for the paper bag.

name: Franz Kafka
essay: It was explained to K. that he had paid for the privilege of being locked inside the small, dimly lit parlor, a circumstance which, though presented to him as a form of amusement, seemed to differ very little from his ordinary working life, except that here the authorities had taken the trouble to paint faux-cracks upon the plaster and hide brass keys inside fake hollowed-out volumes of historical treatises. He sat upon the threadbare sofa, listening to the muffled whispers of his companions who were frantically turning over couch cushions and deciphering numbers scribbled on the backs of framed landscapes, while a hidden clock ticked away minutes that were said to belong to them, though K. suspected that even if they managed to align every symbol correctly before the chime sounded, the door would only open into another hallway where a different attendant, possessing slightly more authority than the youth who had locked them in, would inform them that their liberation was merely provisional and subject to a final audit by the central directorate, who was currently away on business and could not be reached until Monday morning at the earliest. Therefore, he remained seated, refraining from touching the lock, lest an accidental success be interpreted as a request for immediate dismissal.

name: Michel de Montaigne
essay: I am naturally inclined to linger in my bed, where my thoughts settle most agreeably before the demands of the day intrude; yet here is a little brass engine, devised to shatter that quietude by a sudden, violent ringing. I know not what profit a man finds in startling his own soul out of its proper rest: for if slumber be a shadow of death, to wrench ourselves from it by artifice rather than by the gentle invitation of nature seems a kind of daily violence. And yet, I must confess my own weakness; when left to my own humour, I slide so far into sloth that the morning is half spent before I have put on my doublet; so perhaps this noisy fury is a necessary whip for a mind as sluggish as mine. But what a miserable condition it is, to owe our vigilance not to reason or virtue, but to a piece of rattling iron! We mock the slave who moves at the sound of his master's bell, while we place upon our own nightstands a tiny executioner of our ease; or if not an executioner, at least a rude intruder that takes from us that sweet, uncertain borderland between dreaming and waking, where I think I am often wiser than in my full soberness.

name: Michel de Montaigne
object: reclining a seat on a plane
essay: I have so little mastery over my own limbs when confined in narrow quarters that I am forever shifting from cheek to cheek, seeking a repose that my restless nature denies me; yet no sooner do I press that small lever to ease my spine by two inches than I feel a sudden pang of shame, knowing I have stolen that same measure of air from the knees of the unoffending gentleman behind me. And if he, in his turn, should thrust his chair back into my lap, I am presently moved to an unreasonable anger: so prompt are we to pardon in ourselves the very inclinations we condemn in others. For what is this desire to tilt one's frame but a childish refusal of our present condition? Yet I cannot wholly condemn a man for seeking a little respite from this iron stiffness; I have done it myself in moments of weariness, though I never reaped from it the peace I promised my soul. We are so built that our tiny comforts must ever be bought at the expense of our neighbor's misery; and I know not whether to blame the contrivance itself, or rather that restless infirmity of our spirits which makes us prefer an uneasy slope to an honest uprightness.

name: Friedrich Nietzsche
essay: The modern soul demands above all things that love be rendered painless—and in doing so, it destroys the very soil out of which love grows. What is this digital market of faces if not the final triumph of the small man, who trembles at the thought of rejection, of conflict, of the violent collision of two wills? He wishes to select his destiny as one selects a sausage at the butcher: pre-inspected, guaranteed, stripped of all dangerous ambiguity. One flicks a finger, and the troubling mystery of another human being is reduced to a flickering image, a commodity to be approved or dismissed without the slightest expenditure of spirit. This is the morality of the herd made invisible: the total elimination of risk. But where there is no risk, there is no value; where there is no danger, there is only the pathetic comfort of swine huddling together against the frost. You believe you are choosing a partner—in truth, you are merely organizing your own anesthesia. You have traded the terrible magnificence of the encounter for a machine that promises you will never again have to suffer the agony of a gaze that does not look back.

name: Friedrich Nietzsche
essay: To seek out a lock merely for the pleasure of finding its key—that is the final, pathetic refinement of a race that has forgotten how to bleed. The modern coward demands the thrill of the dungeon, but only on the condition that the gaoler holds the clock and guarantees his supper. Observe these voluntary prisoners: they gather in small, eager herds to solve petty riddles constructed by clerks as hollow as themselves; they cheer when a false door springs open, believing they have achieved a triumph of the spirit. It is not liberation they desire, but the illusion of peril without its terrible price. True overcoming is forged only in the furnace of necessity, where failure means ruin and the walls do not part for a fee. But the little man cannot bear necessity—his nerves are too fragile, his soul too soft. He requires a crisis with an appointment: a catastrophe that expires in sixty minutes. He pays his coin for this counterfeit agony so that he may return to his comfortable numbness, persuaded that he has wrestled with fate—when he has merely played at captivity.

name: George Orwell
essay: The main trouble with the airport lounge is that it tries to make a man feel like a gentleman by treating him like an invalid. You pay an extra pound or two at the gate, or hold the right strip of cardboard, and at once you are ushered away from the noise of the main hall into a carpeted box where everything is muted, soft, and slightly warm. The lighting is turned down so low that you can barely read a newspaper, and soft music drips constantly from hidden speakers like water from a leaky tap. There are deep leather armchairs to sink into, but they are designed in such a way that you cannot sit up straight or look your neighbour in the eye. On a long counter sit metal dishes full of lukewarm, yellow soup and dry bread rolls wrapped in cellophane. It is all free, or seems free, which is why middle-class travellers gorge themselves on cheap gin and stale nuts while watching a television screen with the sound turned off. The whole place smells faintly of carpet cleaner and gin. It exists not to give you real comfort, but to sell the illusion that you are better than the crowd outside, when in truth you have merely paid to be penned in a quieter room.

name: George Orwell
essay: If you watch a man at one of these metal tills, you will see that he is doing two things at once: paying for his own bread and doing the shopkeeper's work for him. The shopkeeper saves a wage, and the customer receives nothing in return except the trouble of finding the barcode on a tin of peas. It is sold to us as a convenience, but it is obvious to anyone with eyes that it is merely a device to make the public do for free what used to be paid labor. When you bark at a glass screen because a plastic bag has not registered its proper weight, you are not saving time. You are simply performing a piece of unpaid clerical work under the watchful eye of a bored guard who has been hired to make sure you do not steal the bacon you are already packing yourself. The whole business belongs to that modern habit of pretending that less service is actually more freedom. A hundred years ago, a shopkeeper who asked his customers to weigh their own flour and drop the money into a box would have been thought mad or bankrupt. Today it is called progress, and millions of people step up to the glowing screen every evening, perfectly content to be turned into unpaid shop assistants.

name: Hunter S Thompson
essay: The manager was nineteen years old, possessed the flat, dead eyes of a turnpike toll-collector, and he took forty-five of my dollars before slamming a bolted oak door in my face with the hideous, practiced glee of a small-town hanging judge. There were six of us trapped in that velvet-lined dungeon under the strip mall, surrounded by fake books and brass padlocks that smelled faintly of cheap disinfectant and absolute defeat, while a digital clock on the wall shrieked red numbers down toward zero like a missile launch countdown managed by accountants. I knew instantly that the whole enterprise was a sick psychological experiment funded by the chamber of commerce to train the middle class for permanent incarceration. We were supposed to find a key hidden inside a hollow skull, but my fingers were locking up because some unseen bastard in a back room was watching us through a fish-eye lens and broadcasting recorded thunder through a tinny speaker whenever we touched the wrong lamp. It was a terrifying glimpse into the future of American leisure. People were paying top dollar to simulate their own execution. I kicked the door until my boots cracked, but the lock held firm, and the manager just laughed through the intercom like a hyena on the corporate payroll.

name: Hunter S Thompson
object: reclining a seat on a plane
essay: Thirty thousand feet above the Oklahoma panhandle, the bastard in 14B unleashed a calculated act of violence against my kneecaps. There was a sickening hydraulic hiss, a sharp metallic click, and suddenly two hundred pounds of sweaty synthetic polyester leaned back into my personal airspace with the quiet, unyielding authority of an armored division taking a border town. It is a terrible mechanism, engineered by sadists in corporate boardrooms who realized they could sell six extra inches of legroom back to us if they first turned the economy cabin into a crawling pit of human agony. I stared at the back of his greasy head, mere centimeters from my chin, feeling the raw panic of a trapped animal as my plastic tray table jammed directly into my solar plexus. He didn't even look back. That is the genius of the machine: it converts ordinary middle-management cowardice into a weapon of quiet, passive-aggressive warfare, allowing a man to crush another human being's femur without ever having to look him in the eye. I hit my own button in pure self-defense, plunging the poor doomed soul behind me into the same cramped hell, compounding the misery down the line like a row of falling dominoes in a high-altitude prison ward. We are monsters now.

name: Mark Twain
essay: A man will sit down before this glass slate and spend three hours declaring himself the most modest creature alive, and another four accepting the tearful congratulations of six hundred strangers for having said so. Now, I am no philosopher, nor do I pretend to fathom the deep workings of modern enterprise, but it seems to me that if a fellow were half as indispensable as he claims on his page, he would scarcely have the leisure to compose forty paragraphs on the profound moral lesson he derived from dropping his toast. Yet there they assemble by the million, doffing their caps to one another, each solemn soul certifying that his neighbor is a prodigy of wisdom and a marvel of virtue, though neither would trust the other to guard a brass button. The entire enterprise rests upon a silent contract: if I agree to marvel at your elevation to Assistant Sub-Secretary of Corrugated Box Planning, you will pretend to weep with inspiration over my thoughts on corporate synergy. It is the most meticulously engineered spectacle of mutual flattery ever devised, and I reckon it keeps several million people entirely too busy to perform any useful labor whatever.
